# Getting Started with ContextNet

**ContextNet** extends [NicheNet](https://github.com/saeyslab/nichenetr) by replacing NicheNet's generic gene regulatory network with a **context-specific gene regulatory network (GRN)** inferred from the biological system being studied. In practice, ContextNet asks whether a sender-cell ligand can explain a receiver-cell gene program through regulatory edges that are active in that context.

## Goal of Tutorial 01

This tutorial is a smoke test and object-model walkthrough. It uses a tiny synthetic fixture shipped with the package so a new user can verify that installation works without needing lab-private data. The expected result is simple by design: ligand `TGFB1` should rank above `FGF2` because the toy gene regulatory network connects `TGFB1` more strongly to the receiver target program.

Do not interpret the synthetic result biologically. Use it to learn what files ContextNet expects, what objects it creates, what the printed output should look like, and how to extract tables for downstream analysis.

## What Is a Context-Specific Gene Regulatory Network (GRN)?

A **gene regulatory network (GRN)** describes which transcription factors regulate which target genes and how strongly those regulatory edges are supported. NicheNet includes a generic GRN compiled from public prior knowledge. ContextNet replaces that generic GRN with a context-specific GRN inferred from matched single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq or another upstream regulatory-inference workflow.

This matters because ligand-target prediction depends on the regulatory layer. If the GRN is generic, a ligand can be prioritized through regulatory edges that may not be active in your tissue, disease state, or cell population. If the GRN is context-specific, the ligand-target matrix is constrained by the regulatory relationships observed in the profiled system.

ContextNet expects one of these GRN inputs:

| Input type | What it means | Typical source |
|------------|---------------|----------------|
| target-gene x transcription-factor matrix | Rows are target genes, columns are transcription factors, values are regulatory weights | ContextNet GRN inference pipeline |
| edge table | One row per transcription-factor to target-gene edge | SCENIC+, Pando, custom models |
| package-specific object | Regulatory output already produced by another tool | SCENIC+, Pando |

The package importer normalizes those inputs into a `ContextGRN` object. The upstream ContextNet GRN inference pipeline should be linked from the project documentation when it is public: <https://github.com/settylab/contextnet-pipeline>. If that repository is not yet public, users can still run ContextNet by providing a compatible matrix or edge table.

## Environment and Data Setup

Install ContextNet before starting this tutorial; installation belongs in the repository `README.md` and `vignettes/installation-micromamba.md`, not inside the biological walkthrough. The cells below only load packages, locate the public smoke-test fixture, and print the expected input paths.

Run this notebook from the repository root or from the `notebooks/` directory. The setup cell normalizes the working directory to the repository root so the same notebook works in Jupyter, JupyterLab, `nbconvert`, and RStudio.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_03, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
suppressPackageStartupMessages({
    library(ContextNet)
    library(Seurat)
    library(nichenetr)
    library(ggplot2)
})

HAS_CCFLOWR <- requireNamespace("ccflowR", quietly = TRUE)
if (HAS_CCFLOWR) {
    suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ccflowR))
} else {
    message("ccflowR is not installed; the Sankey visualization cell will be skipped.")
}

theme_set(theme_minimal(base_family = "sans"))
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_04, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
check_ecosystem(verbose = TRUE)
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_05, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
PROJECT_DIR <- normalizePath(getwd(), mustWork = TRUE)
if (basename(PROJECT_DIR) == "notebooks" &&
    file.exists(file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "..", "DESCRIPTION"))) {
    PROJECT_DIR <- normalizePath(file.path(PROJECT_DIR, ".."), mustWork = TRUE)
}
if (!file.exists(file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "DESCRIPTION"))) {
    stop("Run this notebook from the ContextNet repository root or from the notebooks/ directory.")
}
setwd(PROJECT_DIR)
cat("Using project root:", getwd(), "\n")

SMOKE_DIR <- Sys.getenv(
    "CONTEXTNET_SMOKE_DIR",
    unset = file.path(PROJECT_DIR, "inst", "extdata", "contextnet_smoke")
)
GRN_FILE <- file.path(SMOKE_DIR, "gene_x_tf.csv")
SEURAT_FILE <- file.path(SMOKE_DIR, "seurat_obj.rds")
NICHENET_DB <- SMOKE_DIR

SENDER <- c("sender_a", "sender_b")
RECEIVER <- "receiver"
GENESET_OI <- c("SERPINE1", "CDKN1A")
GROUP_COL <- "cell_type"

stopifnot(file.exists(GRN_FILE), file.exists(SEURAT_FILE), dir.exists(NICHENET_DB))
cat("Smoke fixture:", SMOKE_DIR, "\n")
cat("GRN file:", GRN_FILE, "\n")
cat("Seurat file:", SEURAT_FILE, "\n")
cat("Toy NicheNet database:", NICHENET_DB, "\n")
cat("ccflowR available:", HAS_CCFLOWR, "\n")
```

## Step 1: Inspect the Smoke-Test Inputs

The fixture contains all inputs needed for a minimal ContextNet run:

- `gene_x_tf.csv`: a toy context-specific gene regulatory network (GRN).
- `seurat_obj.rds`: a tiny Seurat object with two sender populations, one receiver population, and one reference population.
- `lr_network_human_21122021.rds` and `weighted_networks_nsga2r_final.rds`: tiny NicheNet-compatible prior files.

The fixture is synthetic. It is useful for installation testing because it is small, deterministic, and fully shareable.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_07, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
seurat_obj <- readRDS(SEURAT_FILE)

cat("Seurat object:", nrow(seurat_obj), "genes x", ncol(seurat_obj), "cells\n")
cat("Metadata columns:", paste(colnames(seurat_obj@meta.data), collapse = ", "), "\n")
print(table(seurat_obj[[GROUP_COL]][, 1]))

head(seurat_obj@meta.data)
```

The printed table confirms that the toy object has four cell populations. `sender_a` and `sender_b` express ligands, `receiver` expresses the target program, and `reference` gives a comparison population. In a real analysis, these metadata columns should encode biologically meaningful cell types, conditions, samples, and receiver states.

## Step 2: Import the Context-Specific Gene Regulatory Network (GRN)

`import_grn()` reads the target-gene x transcription-factor matrix and returns a `ContextGRN`. This object stores the regulatory evidence before any NicheNet propagation has happened. At this point, the edges are transcription-factor to target-gene relationships, not ligand-target predictions.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_10, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
grn <- import_grn(GRN_FILE, verbose = TRUE)

cat("Object class:", class(grn), "\n")
cat("Transcription factors:", length(tfs(grn)), "\n")
cat("Target genes:", length(targets(grn)), "\n")
cat("Regulatory edges:", length(grn), "\n")

head(edges(grn))
```

Interpret this output before continuing. A useful `ContextGRN` should have non-zero edges, recognizable transcription-factor symbols, target genes that overlap the expression object, and enough density to propagate signal. In the smoke fixture, the expected edges are `SMAD3 -> SERPINE1/CDKN1A` and `FOS -> MMP1/JUNB`.

## Step 3: Integrate the GRN with NicheNet Priors

`integrate_networks()` combines three layers:

1. ligand-receptor prior edges,
2. intracellular signaling prior edges,
3. the context-specific transcription-factor to target-gene GRN.

The result is a `ContextNetwork`. Its central data structure is a ligand-target matrix: rows are target genes, columns are ligands, and values are propagated regulatory-potential scores. This object is reusable across many sender/receiver questions from the same biological context.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_13, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
network <- integrate_networks(
    grn,
    nichenet_database = NICHENET_DB,
    mode = "replace",
    damping_factor = 0.5,
    ltf_cutoff = 0,
    verbose = TRUE
)

ltm <- ligand_target_matrix(network)
cat("Object class:", class(network), "\n")
cat("Ligand-target matrix:", nrow(ltm), "targets x", ncol(ltm), "ligands\n")
round(ltm[c("SERPINE1", "CDKN1A", "MMP1", "JUNB"), , drop = FALSE], 3)
```

The matrix should show stronger `TGFB1` weights for `SERPINE1` and `CDKN1A`, and stronger `FGF2` weights for `MMP1` and `JUNB`. That is the built-in positive control for this smoke test. In a real dataset, the same matrix is the ContextNet-specific replacement for NicheNet's default ligand-target matrix.

## Step 4: Predict Ligand Activity for One Receiver Program

For the smoke test, we provide the receiver target genes directly with `geneset_oi = c("SERPINE1", "CDKN1A")`. This avoids running differential expression on a toy object and makes the expected output deterministic. In a real analysis, you can either pass a curated receiver gene set or let ContextNet compute differentially expressed genes from a cell-type or condition comparison.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_16, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
result <- predict_ligand_activity_nichenet(
    object = seurat_obj,
    network = network,
    sender = SENDER,
    receiver = RECEIVER,
    geneset_oi = GENESET_OI,
    group_col = GROUP_COL,
    top_n_ligands = 2,
    top_n_targets = 4,
    nichenet_database = NICHENET_DB,
    verbose = TRUE
)

cat("Object class:", class(result), "\n")
cat("Top ligands:", paste(top_ligands(result), collapse = ", "), "\n")
cat("Top targets:", paste(top_targets(result), collapse = ", "), "\n")

ligand_activities(result)
```

The expected top ligand is `TGFB1`. The most important columns are:

- `test_ligand`: the candidate upstream ligand being scored.
- `aupr`: area under the precision-recall curve for recovering the receiver gene set. Higher values mean the ligand's predicted targets better recover the target program.
- `aupr_corrected`: AUPR after correcting for the baseline positive rate.
- `pearson`: correlation between predicted ligand-target regulatory potential and the receiver gene-set label.

For this fixture, `TGFB1` is intentionally connected to `SERPINE1` and `CDKN1A`, so it should rank above `FGF2`.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_18, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
ligand_target_links(result)
```

The ligand-target link table explains why the ligand ranked highly. In the smoke fixture, `TGFB1 -> SERPINE1` and `TGFB1 -> CDKN1A` have higher regulatory-potential weights than the corresponding `FGF2` links. In a real analysis, inspect this table before making biological claims from a ranked ligand list.

## Step 5: Visualize the Main Outputs

The bar plot summarizes ligand activity. The heatmap-like tile plot shows which ligand-target links support the ranking. These plots are intentionally simple so the smoke-test output is easy to compare across installations.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_21, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
activities <- ligand_activities(result)
activities$test_ligand <- factor(
    activities$test_ligand,
    levels = rev(activities$test_ligand[order(activities$aupr)])
)

ggplot(activities, aes(x = aupr, y = test_ligand)) +
    geom_col(fill = "#3B6FB6") +
    labs(
        x = "Ligand activity (AUPR)",
        y = "Ligand",
        title = "Smoke test ligand ranking"
    )
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_22, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
links <- ligand_target_links(result)

ggplot(links, aes(x = ligand, y = target, fill = weight)) +
    geom_tile(color = "white") +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "#F2F2F2", high = "#2166AC") +
    labs(
        x = "Ligand",
        y = "Receiver target gene",
        fill = "Regulatory potential",
        title = "Ligand-target support for the smoke-test program"
    )
```

## Optional Path-Level Visualization with ccflowR

`ccflowR` is an optional visualization package for Sankey or river plots of cell-cell communication. It helps when a table of ligand activities is no longer enough: for example, when you want to see which sender cell types, ligands, receptors, and receiver cells form the highest-priority paths.

ContextNet prepares the path table with `prepare_for_ccflowr()` and `combine_sankey_data()`. If `ccflowR` is not installed, the core ContextNet analysis still works; only this visualization is skipped.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_24, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
sankey_raw <- prepare_for_ccflowr(
    result,
    expression_data = seurat_obj,
    network = network,
    top_n_ligands = 2,
    group_col = GROUP_COL,
    min_cells = 5
)
sankey_data <- combine_sankey_data(sankey_raw, threshold_quantile = 0)

cat("ccflowR input rows:", nrow(sankey_data), "\n")
head(sankey_data)
```

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_25, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
if (HAS_CCFLOWR) {
    cell_colors <- c(
        sender_a = "#3B6FB6", sender_b = "#8B5A2B",
        receiver = "#2F8F5B", reference = "#999999"
    )

    suppressMessages(
        ccflowR::sankey_plot(sankey_data, colors = cell_colors) +
            ccflowR::sankey_colors(by = "receiver") +
            ccflowR::sankey_alpha(0.65) +
            ccflowR::sankey_title("ContextNet smoke-test paths") +
            ccflowR::sankey_font(family = "Arial", size = 12) +
            ccflowR::sankey_layout(width = 760, height = 520)
    )
} else {
    message("Skipping Sankey plot because ccflowR is not installed.")
}
```

Read the Sankey plot as a prioritized path-level hypothesis, not as proof of physical communication. A real path needs additional support from ligand expression, receptor expression, spatial proximity, perturbation, or orthogonal validation.

## Object Model Summary

ContextNet uses three main S4 objects. The important point is that each object answers a different question.

| Object | Created by | Question it answers | What to inspect |
|--------|------------|--------------------|-----------------|
| `ContextGRN` | `import_grn()` | What regulatory edges are active in this context? | `edges()`, `tfs()`, `targets()`, `regulons()` |
| `ContextNetwork` | `integrate_networks()` | How do ligands propagate to target genes through this context-specific network? | `ligand_target_matrix()`, `ligands()`, `integration_params()` |
| `ContextResult` | `predict_ligand_activity_nichenet()` | Which ligands explain this receiver gene program? | `ligand_activities()`, `top_ligands()`, `ligand_target_links()`, `parameters()` |

The code below prints compact summaries of those objects so you can compare your local output with the expected shape.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_28, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
object_summary <- list(
    ContextGRN = list(
        class = class(grn),
        n_edges = length(grn),
        n_tfs = length(tfs(grn)),
        n_targets = length(targets(grn))
    ),
    ContextNetwork = list(
        class = class(network),
        ltm_dim = paste(dim(ligand_target_matrix(network)), collapse = " x "),
        ligands = paste(ligands(network), collapse = ", "),
        mode = integration_params(network)$mode
    ),
    ContextResult = list(
        class = class(result),
        top_ligands = paste(top_ligands(result), collapse = ", "),
        n_ligand_activity_rows = nrow(ligand_activities(result)),
        n_ligand_target_links = nrow(ligand_target_links(result))
    )
)

object_summary
```

## What to Do Next

If this notebook runs successfully, the installation is functional for the core ContextNet workflow. Next steps depend on your data:

- Use Tutorial 02 when you have a real Seurat object and a context-specific GRN and want a single-tissue, receiver-state analysis.
- Use Tutorial 03 when you have biological replicates and need sample-aware MultiNicheNet prioritization.
- Replace the smoke-test `gene_x_tf.csv` with your own context-specific gene regulatory network (GRN), and replace the smoke-test Seurat object with your expression object.

```{r 01_getting_started_cell_30, message=TRUE, warning=TRUE}
session_pkgs <- c("ContextNet", "Seurat", "nichenetr", "multinichenetr", "ggplot2", "ccflowR")
cat("R version:", R.version.string, "\n")
for (pkg in session_pkgs) {
    if (requireNamespace(pkg, quietly = TRUE)) {
        cat(pkg, "version:", as.character(utils::packageVersion(pkg)), "\n")
    } else {
        cat(pkg, "version: not installed\n")
    }
}
```
